newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy grows but unemployment still high.
newsitem.headline: German economy grows but unemployment still high.

text.p: The German economy rebounded more strongly than expected in the second quarter of the year, official data showed on Thursday, but continued high unemployment in August left little reason for cheer.

Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1.5 percent from the first quarter and 1.2 percent from the year-earlier quarter, after shrinking 0.5 percent in the first quarter from the quarter before and only growing 0.2 percent year-on-year.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said full-year growth for 1996 could well be stronger than the government's previous forecast of 0.75 percent.
The good news of the rebound was partly overshadowed by the more recent unemployment data, which showed continued weakness.

The number of jobless rose 14,000 to 3.939 million last month on a seasonally adjusted basis, the Federal Labour Office said. The adjusted unemployment rate was unchanged at 10.3 percent of the workforce.
Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said September data should show a seasonal improvement over August but the economic upturn was unlikely to have an immediate impact on unemployment.
"Unemployment figures tend to be a late indicator and we know it won't be just a couple of weeks (before we see an impact)," Jagoda told a news conference.
Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said the fight against unemployment remained Chancellor Helmut Kohl's most important domestic goal.
"But this will not be achieved without austerity measures," Hausmann said. "The Programme for More Jobs and Growth will be steadily implemented."
Unions have slated mass protests in several major cities this weekend against the government's unpopular savings measures, which they say will boost, not reduce, joblessness.

Rexrodt said low interest rates, moderate wage agreements, stable prices and a retreat in the mark's overvaluation all contributed to a recovery of business confidence in the second quarter. Growth in the first half of the year was 0.7 percent from the year-earlier half, he said.
Uwe Angenendt of BHF Bank told Reuters Financial Television the second-quarter growth figures were "on the upper end of expectations. It is quite good news for the German economy".

Juergen Stanowsky of Dresdner Bank was even more bullish. "For all of 1996, we still expect a growth rate of 1.5 percent. The inflation perspective is quite good. There is no reason for the Bundesbank to cut rates," Stanowsky said.

Economist Mathias Hafner of BZW took a slightly more sceptical view. "The numbers are good but we believe that growth will normalise in the second half of the year and give the Bundesbank little reason to do anything else on interest rates. For the second half we expect more moderate growth, around 0.5 percent on the quarter."
West Germany showed growth of 1.0 percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter, according to the Economics Ministry, and 1.1 percent from the year-earlier quarter.
East Germany grew a vigorous 5.0 percent from the previous quarter and 2.6 percent from the year-earlier period.

Seasonally adjusted unemployment in west Germany rose 26,000 to 2.806 million in August and the jobless rate was steady at 9.0 percent. In east Germany the number of jobless fell 12,000 to 1.133 million. The unemployment rate was 15.0 percent, down from 15.4 percent.
